newsitem.title: UK: UK Referendum Party pitches for Moslem vote.
newsitem.headline: UK Referendum Party pitches for Moslem vote.

text.p: The setting was slightly surreal.

On a rainy day at a south London mosque, an Anglo-French billionaire is warning a few dozen Moslems, many of them Pakistani immigrants, of the dangers of Britain being swallowed up by a European superstate.
After listening to a prayer from the Koran, Sir James Goldsmith, founder of the Referendum Party and a man who can call Britain one of his homes, warms to his theme.
Britain, he said, was on the verge of giving up powers over its foreign policy, defence and currency to a degenerate bureaucracy in Brussels that would reduce it to the status of a servile province.
Surely, he implored, it was only just that Britons should be allowed a referendum to decide their fate?
"The idea that the British people cannot have a say on this radical change eliminating all the points that make up our sovereignty is intolerable.

"They have been giving it away not only without our approval, but secretly with lies. It is the assassination of a nation," says the businessman-turned-politician, who is fighting the London constituency of Putney in Thursday's poll.

In an election campaign where many voters complain they can barely distinguish between the two main parties, Conservative and Labour, Goldsmith offers a bracing, one-issue alternative. The party would disband once it had achieved its goal, he vows.
The Referendum Party briefly had a member of the last parliament when George Gardiner defected from the Conservatives.

But single-issue parties have never flourished in Britain and opinion polls give it no chance under Britain's first-past- the-post voting system of winning any more seats -- its nationwide support is around two or three percent.

However, this masks pockets of strength, notably in coastal communities angry over the European Union's fisheries policy, that could make the difference between re-election and defeat for a number of Conservatives.

Goldsmith's crusade has undoubtedly reinforced a general trend toward "Euro-scepticism" in British politics that has led both main parties virtually to rule out joining the EU's planned single currency in the next five years.
But Goldsmith, whose mother was French, bristles at the suggestion that hostility to deeper European integration could grow into an ugly nationalism or xenophobia.
"I think it's a single state that will lead to xenophobia," he told Reuters after his speech.

"I've always said it would create centrifugal forces that would destroy it and destroy the European dream. I have always been -- and this makes people laugh -- strongly pro-European, and remain it, but pro a Europe of nations.

"That is the only Europe that can be created from which can emerge a strong Europe. I do not believe that a bureaucratic one... dominated by one nation (Germany) can work. Our people will not accept it," he added.

With women hidden behind a screen from their menfolk, Goldsmith tried to woo his Moslem audience by warning that a centralised Europe would be hostile to the small businesses many of them had toiled to build up.
The questions on Europe suggested he is not without support among the 3,000-strong Ahmadiyya community.
But the Moslem voters also wanted to know what Goldsmith would do about their most pressing issue - the local council's refusal to give planning permission for a bigger mosque.
"We are having to pray in the rain," an elderly man told him. "We are suffering."
Goldsmith did not answer. He had come to talk about Europe.
